The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: The entries of $U^*U-I_2$ and $\det U-1$ are continuous real polynomial functions of the eight real coordinates of $U$. Their common zero set $SU(2)$ is therefore closed. Since $U^*U=I_2$, each column of $U$ has Euclidean norm one, so every matrix entry has modulus at most one; hence $SU(2)$ is bounded in $\mathbb R^8$. By [F2], $SU(2)$ is compact. Its real Lie-group structure is supplied by [F1].

The matrices $g=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$ and
$h=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfy $g^*g=h^*h=I_2$ and
$\det g=\det h=1$, so both lie in $SU(2)$. Direct multiplication gives
$gh=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$hg=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}$; therefore $gh\ne hg$ and the group is noncommutative.

By [F1], every element of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the form
$\begin{pmatrix}i\alpha&z\\-\overline z&-i\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ with
$\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $z\in\mathbb C$. Thus $T_1,T_2,T_3$ form a real
basis. Multiplying the displayed matrices gives
$[T_1,T_2]=T_3$, $[T_2,T_3]=T_1$, and $[T_3,T_1]=T_2$; antisymmetry and
bilinearity give the stated $\epsilon_{abc}$ formula.

The same finite matrix products give
$-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(T_aT_b)=\delta_{ab}$. Since each $X\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$
has real coordinates in this basis, $\kappa(X,X)$ is the sum of their squares,
and $\kappa$ is positive definite; trace cyclicity gives symmetry. For every
$g\in SU(2)$,
$\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_gX,\operatorname{Ad}_gY)
=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(gXYg^{-1})
=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)=\kappa(X,Y)$, so the form is
$\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant.

coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ of length, orientation
$dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, time orientation of increasing
$x^0$, and Lorentz metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Use
$c=\hbar=1$, so $x^0=t$, the coordinate and spacetime lengths have unit
$\mathrm m$, and the natural action $S/\hbar$ is dimensionless.

instance selects a smooth right principal $SU(2)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and
admits only its bundle sector $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The matter-representation label set
is empty, so there are no matter fields or current source. The Lie algebra is
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with basis $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2$ and positive
$\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant form

$\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$. The positive coupling $g_{\mathrm{YM}}$ is a
fixed dimensionless model parameter.

$SU(2)$ action on each fibre and equivariant local trivializations; a global
section is not part of the datum. The sector $[P]$ is the nonempty minimum-rank set code of its smooth equivariant bundle-isomorphism type over $M$, in the supplied non-Abelian gauge-data convention. The gauge group $\mathcal G(P)$ consists of smooth
diffeomorphisms $\Phi:P\to P$ with $\pi\circ\Phi=\pi$ and
$\Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g$. A gauge function $U_i\to SU(2)$ is only a local
description unless a global trivialization has been specified.

section $s_i:U_i\to P$, let $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and let

alternating-form extension of the Lie bracket, and the local forms on
overlaps satisfy the right-action transition convention
$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+g_{ij}^{-1}dg_{ij}$ and
$F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i$ when $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$. Define the
real adjoint vector bundle by
$$\operatorname{ad}(P):=(P\times\mathfrak{su}(2))/\sim,\qquad\text{where }\sim\text{ is generated by }(pg,Z)\sim(p,\operatorname{Ad}_g Z).$$

of a smooth section $\eta$ are maps $\eta_i:U_i\to\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and obey

$\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i)$ a global scalar four-form.

Write $\Omega^k(M)$ for the space of smooth real $k$-forms on $M$. For
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(M)$, write
$\alpha=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k}
dx^{\mu_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{\mu_k}$, raise indices using $\eta^{-1}$
and set
$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k},\qquad\operatorname{vol}_\eta:=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3.$$
For $0\le k\le4$, define the Lorentzian Hodge map
$*_\eta:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ as the unique smooth fibrewise-linear
map satisfying $\alpha\wedge *_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta
\operatorname{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(M)$. The
nondegenerate metric-induced pairing and the wedge pairing give this unique
map pointwise, and the constant coefficients make it smooth. On
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued forms it acts on the spacetime-form factor.

Adopt the local Lorentzian action density

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{YM}}(A_i)\,d^4x=-\frac{1}{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\,\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i),\qquad [A_i]=\mathrm m^{-1},\quad [F_i]=\mathrm m^{-2}.
$$

action is its integral. On all of $M$, the action is defined when that
integral converges. Local stationarity is tested through relative action
differences under smooth compactly supported adjoint-bundle-valued
one-form variations; these differences have compact support and are finite.
No boundary values are imposed at infinity. On a finite region, admissible
variations vanish near its boundary. This is an adopted classical model and
normalization, not a theorem, measured law, or claim that a quantum
continuum theory exists.

$T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $a\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $G$ is compact and
noncommutative, its real Lie algebra has basis $T_1,T_2,T_3$ with
$[T_a,T_b]=\sum_{c=1}^3\epsilon_{abc}T_c$, and the real bilinear form
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is positive
definite, symmetric, and invariant under
$\operatorname{Ad}_gX=gXg^{-1}$, with $\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$.

Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle as in
[[def-smooth-principal-g-bundle]]. A **smooth gauge transformation** of $P$ is
a smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi:P\to P$ satisfying
$$\pi\circ\Phi=\pi,\qquad \Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g\quad(p\in P,\ g\in G).$$
Here diffeomorphism has the meaning of
[[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]. The **gauge
group** $\mathcal G(P)$ is the set of these transformations under composition.
The identity is a smooth diffeomorphism and composites of smooth maps are
smooth by
[[prop-identity-maps-and-composites-of-smooth-maps-are-smooth]]; composites of
diffeomorphisms are diffeomorphisms because their inverses are composites of
the smooth inverses. The identity covers $M$ and commutes with the right
action. If $\Phi,\Psi\in\mathcal G(P)$, then $\Phi\circ\Psi$ covers $M$ and
$(\Phi\circ\Psi)(pg)=\Phi(\Psi(p)g)=\Phi(\Psi(p))g$, so the conditions are
closed under composition. The inverse of such a $\Phi$ also covers $M$: if
$q=\Phi(p)$ then $\pi(\Phi^{-1}(q))=\pi(p)=\pi(q)$. Equivariance gives
$$\Phi^{-1}(qg)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(p)g)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(pg))=pg.$$

group under the composition law of [[def-group]].

The structure group $G$ acts on each fibre of $P$, while $\mathcal G(P)$ acts
on the total bundle by automorphisms over the identity map of $M$. They are
different groups: a gauge transformation may vary from fibre to fibre, and
this definition assigns no topology or finite-dimensional Lie-group structure

curvatures from

$X,Y\in T_pP$,
$$K_{\Phi_*H}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY)=d\Phi_p(K_H(X,Y)).$$

principal connections.

The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$A^u=u^{-1}du$. Since $u=\exp(T_3\sin(x^0/\ell))$ and $T_3$ commutes with itself, differentiation yields

the same formula would give the zero potential; the chosen sine has
nonzero derivative, so $A^u$ is nonzero.

Each instance of the adopted classical pure Yang–Mills model has spacetime $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$,
coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ of length, orientation
$dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, time orientation of increasing
$x^0$, and Lorentz metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Use
$c=\hbar=1$, so $x^0=t$, the coordinate and spacetime lengths have unit
$\mathrm m$, and the natural action $S/\hbar$ is dimensionless.

Fix the global structure group $G=SU(2)$, not its quotient $SO(3)$. Each
instance selects a smooth right principal $SU(2)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and
admits only its bundle sector $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The matter-representation label set
is empty, so there are no matter fields or current source. The Lie algebra is
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with basis $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2$ and positive
$\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant form
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$, normalized by
$\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$. The positive coupling $g_{\mathrm{YM}}$ is a
fixed dimensionless model parameter.

A smooth right principal bundle here has a free and transitive smooth right
$SU(2)$ action on each fibre and equivariant local trivializations; a global
section is not part of the datum. The sector $[P]$ is the nonempty minimum-rank set code of its smooth equivariant bundle-isomorphism type over $M$, in the supplied non-Abelian gauge-data convention. The gauge group $\mathcal G(P)$ consists of smooth
diffeomorphisms $\Phi:P\to P$ with $\pi\circ\Phi=\pi$ and
$\Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g$. A gauge function $U_i\to SU(2)$ is only a local
description unless a global trivialization has been specified.

A principal connection is a smooth right-invariant horizontal complement
$TP=VP\oplus H$. A gauge field is its connection form $\omega$ with
$\omega(Z_P)=Z$ and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$, where
$R_g(p)=pg$ and
$Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_{SU(2)}(tZ)$. In a local
section $s_i:U_i\to P$, let $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and let
$F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$ be its curvature. Here the bracket is the
alternating-form extension of the Lie bracket, and the local forms on
overlaps satisfy the right-action transition convention
$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+g_{ij}^{-1}dg_{ij}$ and
$F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i$ when $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$. Define the
real adjoint vector bundle by
$$\operatorname{ad}(P):=(P\times\mathfrak{su}(2))/\sim,\qquad\text{where }\sim\text{ is generated by }(pg,Z)\sim(p,\operatorname{Ad}_g Z).$$
For each local section $s_i$, use the smooth vector-bundle chart
$[s_i(x)h,Z]\mapsto(x,\operatorname{Ad}_h Z)$. Consequently, the components
of a smooth section $\eta$ are maps $\eta_i:U_i\to\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and obey
$\eta_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}\eta_i$ when $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$.
Thus $F_i$ represents one global section of $\Lambda^2T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}(P)$,
and the invariant form $\kappa$ makes
$\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i)$ a global scalar four-form.

Write $\Omega^k(M)$ for the space of smooth real $k$-forms on $M$. For
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(M)$, write
$\alpha=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k}
dx^{\mu_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{\mu_k}$, raise indices using $\eta^{-1}$
and set
$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\ldots\mu_k},\qquad\operatorname{vol}_\eta:=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3.$$
For $0\le k\le4$, define the Lorentzian Hodge map
$*_\eta:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ as the unique smooth fibrewise-linear
map satisfying $\alpha\wedge *_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta
\operatorname{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(M)$. The
nondegenerate metric-induced pairing and the wedge pairing give this unique
map pointwise, and the constant coefficients make it smooth. On
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued forms it acts on the spacetime-form factor.

Adopt the local Lorentzian action density

$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{YM}}(A_i)\,d^4x=-\frac{1}{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\,\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i),\qquad [A_i]=\mathrm m^{-1},\quad [F_i]=\mathrm m^{-2}.
$$

For any relatively compact region on which the density is integrable, the
action is its integral. On all of $M$, the action is defined when that
integral converges. Local stationarity is tested through relative action
differences under smooth compactly supported adjoint-bundle-valued
one-form variations; these differences have compact support and are finite.
No boundary values are imposed at infinity. On a finite region, admissible
variations vanish near its boundary. This is an adopted classical model and
normalization, not a theorem, measured law, or claim that a quantum
continuum theory exists.

Assume the axiom of countable choice. Let
$G=SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$ with its real Lie-group
structure. Define the Pauli matrices
$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and put
$T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $a\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $G$ is compact and
noncommutative, its real Lie algebra has basis $T_1,T_2,T_3$ with
$[T_a,T_b]=\sum_{c=1}^3\epsilon_{abc}T_c$, and the real bilinear form
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is positive
definite, symmetric, and invariant under
$\operatorname{Ad}_gX=gXg^{-1}$, with $\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

Use the adopted pure $SU(2)$ model on oriented, time-oriented Minkowski
$\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, no matter fields,
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$, and fixed $g_{\mathrm{YM}}>0$.
For a local section $s_i:U_i\to P$, write
$A_i=s_i^*\omega$,
$F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$, and
$D_{A_i}\eta=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$ for an
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued differential form $\eta$. A smooth local
variation is any $a\in\Omega^1(U_i,\mathfrak{su}(2))$ with compact support
in $U_i$; it represents a global adjoint-bundle-valued connection variation
by extension by zero. Define its dimensionless relative action difference by
$$
\Delta(S/\hbar)_i(\varepsilon;a)=-\frac{1}{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\int_{U_i}\left(\kappa(F_{A_i+\varepsilon a}\wedge *_\eta F_{A_i+\varepsilon a})-\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i)\right).
$$
The integrand difference is compactly supported, so this relative integral is
defined even if the unvaried action over all of $M$ diverges.

The connection is stationary when the derivative at $\varepsilon=0$ of
$\Delta(S/\hbar)_i(\varepsilon;a)$ vanishes for every such variation in every
local trivialization.
It is stationary if and only if
$D_{A_i}(*_\eta F_i)=0$ in every local section. The local equations transform
by the adjoint action on overlaps and therefore define the global,
source-free Yang–Mills equation on the selected bundle sector. This
equivalence is a conditional classical deduction from the adopted action
and compact-support boundary convention.

derivations.claim:
Write $q=x^0-x^3$. Since the coefficient depends only on $q$,
$dA=T_3(b/\ell)\cos(q/\ell)(dx^0-dx^3)\wedge dx^1$. The bracket term
vanishes because $[T_3,T_3]=0$, so this is $F$; it is not identically zero
because $b\ne0$; if $b=0$, both the potential and curvature vanish.

The Lorentzian Hodge operator for the stated orientation gives
$*_\eta((dx^0-dx^3)\wedge dx^1)=-(dx^0-dx^3)\wedge dx^2$. Hence
$*_\eta F=-T_3(b/\ell)\cos(q/\ell)(dx^0-dx^3)\wedge dx^2$. Its exterior
derivative vanishes because differentiating its coefficient contributes a
factor $(dx^0-dx^3)$ already present in the wedge product; the covariant
bracket term also vanishes because both Lie-algebra factors are $T_3$.
Thus $D_A(*_\eta F)=0$. The same repeated null one-form gives
$F\wedge *_\eta F=0$, so the action density vanishes.

By [F4] and step 2.1, the connection is stationary under every
admissible compactly supported variation. The curvature is nonzero by step 1.1, so this is a nontrivial classical solution with zero Lorentzian
quadratic density.
